1.pericope_label: The judgment of the great whore that sitteth upon many waters

schools.summary: Note first that it is fitting for one of the seven angels who held the bowls to explain the judgment on Babylon which has already been pronounced, and that the word used for that judgment is the one employed of Babylon's doom in the Greek of Jeremiah; the genitive is objective, so that it is the judgment upon the harlot and not one she pronounces. Treat the chapter as an explanatory episode in which the action is deliberately delayed so that the power about to be judged may first be described. Then establish the ground before going further. Babylon was the great city whose splendour dazzled and whose power destroyed Jerusalem, against whom the prophets lifted their voices as the embodiment of splendid vice and resistless power, the glory of kingdoms, the golden city which exalted her throne above the stars of God and sat as a lady given to pleasures. In her greatness and her hostility she became the type of later world-powers, so that in this vision Babylon is no longer the literal Babylon but the power which has taken her place of pride and empire, and that power was Rome, which was then what Babylon had been, the hammer of the whole earth and the golden cup that made all the earth drunken. Enter the caution at once, however, for it governs the whole chapter: the very freedom with which the seer transfers to the Rome of his own day the language earlier prophets had applied to ancient Babylon ought to warn us against limited and local interpretations. Support the identification from the detail about many waters, since Babylon drew its wealth by the Euphrates and its irrigation canals while Rome had no such system, so that the item is transferred to the New Babylon rather than literally described; and recall that Nineveh was called a harlot before her, and Tyre also. On the second verse, take the fornication of the kings in its political sense, as the purchasing of Rome's favour by accepting her suzerainty and with it her vices and idolatries, and render the drunkenness as a losing of reason and self-control from the wine, the delicious and delirious draught of her fornication.

Ask first which of the seven angels is meant, since the text does not say. It may be the first of them; one interpreter has argued for the fifth, because his vial was poured upon the seat of the beast, who is the very power here described; but it is better to take it for the seventh and last, as the angel concerned in the utter destruction of antichrist, and therefore the fit one to propose showing the judgment of the great whore. Then identify the kings who committed fornication with her, and do not leave the term vague: these are the ten kings who, being of one mind and one religion, gave their power and strength and kingdom to the beast, and were enticed by her to commit spiritual fornication, that is, idolatry, worshipping as she enjoins the images of gold and silver and brass and wood. From this it appears that she is no mean strumpet but one of great note, sought after and made use of by the great men of the earth. Keep the doctrinal weight on the word fornication, since the whole figure turns on it: idolatrous worship is what is meant, and the covenant broken is the same covenant that betrothed a people to God, so that the offence is treachery and not merely uncleanness. Let the reader feel the scale of what is charged before any application is made of it, for a city which can make the kings of the earth her clients, and the common people drunk on her cup, is not being accused of a private vice but of an empire built on one.

Observe that this vision and the later one of the bride of the Lamb are introduced in the very same words, and take the repetition as a token of the exact opposition between them, the one being the counterpart and contradiction of the other. Note also that the woman sits as a queen, in pomp, power, ease and luxury, and that the many waters on which she sits are many peoples and nations, as the angel afterwards explains. Then say what the figure of the harlot means in Scripture generally, since it is not peculiar to this place: idolatrous worship is frequently represented under the character of a whore or of whoredom, as is evident from numerous passages, and she is called a great whore to denote her excessive depravity and the artful nature of her idolatry, and is seen sitting upon many waters to show the vast extent of her influence. On the second verse, take the fornication of the kings as their partaking of her idolatry and various wickedness, and the inhabitants of the earth as the common people. Then press the drunkenness with a comparison the hearer will feel: no wine can more thoroughly intoxicate those who drink it than false zeal does the followers of the great whore. Add the sober judgment on the state of things this implies, that it is an awful picture of the religion of the world in subjection to such a power, when kings have committed spiritual fornication with her and their subjects have drunk deep, dreadfully deep, into the doctrine of her errors. And where an interpreter cannot see his way clear, let him say so, and not pretend to explain what he does not understand, leaving his readers at liberty to reject his exposition and adopt another, since God alone knows all the secrets of his own wisdom.

Take this as a new vision, not new in its matter, for that is contemporary with what came under the three last vials, but new in the manner of the description. Observe the invitation given to the apostle to view what is to be represented, and mark that the name given her is a name of great infamy. A whore, in this passage, is one that is married and has been false to her husband's bed, one that has forsaken the guide of her youth and broken the covenant of God; and she had been a prostitute to the kings of the earth, whom she had intoxicated with the wine of her fornication. Then take the appearance she made, which was gay and gaudy, as suits such creatures: she was arrayed in purple and scarlet colour, and decked with gold and precious stones and pearls, so that here were all the allurements of worldly honour and riches, pomp and pride, suited to sensual and worldly minds. Take next her principal seat and residence, upon the beast that had seven heads and ten horns, that is to say, the city on seven hills, infamous for idolatry, tyranny and blasphemy. Then her name, which was written on her forehead, for it was the custom of impudent harlots to hang out signs with their names, that all might know what they were. Observe in this that she is named from her place of residence, Babylon the great; but that we may not take it for the old Babylon literally so called, we are told there is a mystery in the name, and it is some other great city resembling the old one. Observe too that she is named from her practice, not only a harlot but a mother of harlots, breeding up harlots and training them to idolatry, the parent and nurse of all false religion.

Read the vision spiritually before reading it politically, and let the woman stand for what she is in the soul before she is located on a map. The multitude of the lost which left the Creator, and prostituted itself to commit adultery with demons, is spoken of as sitting upon the waves, that is, upon the discord of the peoples; and the contrary is to be set beside it at once, that of the multitude of the believers there was one heart and one soul, whom the Apostle espoused to one husband, to present them a pure virgin to Christ. So the waters are not merely nations but the restlessness and division of nations, and the woman sits upon that division because it is what carries her. Take the kings and the inhabitants of the earth on the same principle. The whole is superior to its parts, and by the king and the inhabitants of the earth are meant all those who seek proudly for earthly things, whom the allurement of the world defiles through the lust of vices, and whom madness of the mind makes drunk. Note that the drunkenness needs no cup but the world, and that it is the mind's own madness which completes it. Then let the desert into which the seer is carried be understood as the absence of Deity, whose presence is paradise; and let the beast be the devil, blood-stained through ungodliness, blasphemous, inflated with the arrogance of presumption, who extols the corruption of the wicked. So the whole scene may be read as the state of a soul that has left God, and the reader will find the application nearer home than any identification of cities can make it.

sides.position: Rome of the seer's own day, which had taken Babylon's place of pride and empire; yet the freedom with which the older prophetic language is transferred to her warns against merely local interpretations

Rome, though the identification is loose rather than literal, since Babylon drew her wealth by the Euphrates and its canals while Rome had no such system, so the image is transferred; Nineveh and Tyre had been called harlots before
The Church of Rome, whose influence held the princes of Europe through the dark ages
Not a city at all but the multitude of the lost who left the Creator, sitting upon the waves because the waves are the discord of the peoples

debates.question: Which of the seven angels speaks?

sides.position: The seventh and last, as the angel concerned in the utter destruction of antichrist; Brightman's argument for the fifth, whose vial fell on the seat of the beast, is reported and set aside
It is simply fitting that one of the bowl-bearing angels should explain a judgment already pronounced

outliers.note: Alone declines to expound the chapter in his own person, printing instead the fullest exposition he has met with, telling his readers they are at perfect liberty to reject it and adopt any other, and closing the disclaimer with the remark that God alone knows all the secrets of his own wisdom.

Alone reads the whole scene morally rather than geographically, taking the harlot for the multitude of the lost, the waters for the discord of the peoples, and the wilderness for the absence of Deity whose presence is paradise, and setting against her the believers who were of one heart and one soul.

with whom the kings of the earth have committed fornication
the inhabitants of the earth have been made drunk with the wine of her fornication

3.pericope_label: The woman upon a scarlet coloured beast; MYSTERY, BABYLON THE GREAT

schools.summary: Render the opening better as, and he carried me away into a wilderness in spirit, and note that the verb is used elsewhere of angels bearing a man away at death or in an ecstasy. Ask why the scene is a desert, since the text does not say. Isaiah twice calls Babylon a desert, so the seer may be shown the city's fate under that figure, or may himself be standing in the waste this side of her and looking on. Better still, take the contrast as the point: the woman is splendid and her surroundings desolate, and she may be set against the woman clothed with the sun who was driven into a wilderness and there persecuted but not forsaken, since this one, amid all her dazzling surroundings, is still in a wilderness. Note the change in the symbolism, that in the earlier vision the beast had the seven heads while here the woman riding the beast has them, and that the names of blasphemy which then stood on the heads now cover the whole body; set that against the living creatures who teemed with eyes, the tokens of ready obedience and true intelligence, where this creature teems with tokens of lawlessness and self-sufficiency. On the attire, explain the purple as the dye obtained from a shell-fish of the Mediterranean coasts, much prized and worn by persons of rank, and note that it holds more blue than the crimson though the limits are not accurately defined and the two words are sometimes interchanged, one Gospel calling the mock robe purple where another calls it scarlet. Render decked as gilded, and note that the verb occurs nowhere else in the New Testament. On the cup, recall that Jeremiah called Babylon a golden cup in the hand of the Lord, and that this one, splendid and attractive, is full of a power which robs men of their senses. On the forehead, note that Roman harlots wore a label bearing their names on their brows, and that Christ has a name upon his garment while the redeemed bear God's name on their foreheads. Take the word mystery as a direction to the reader, that Babylon is to be read mystically, and object to the printing in capitals, since nothing in the original answers to it; render rather that a name was written, a mysterious name, the mystery lying in the words Babylon and mother being symbolical and not in the thing itself.

Be clear at the outset that the carrying away was visionary and not bodily. John was not removed from Patmos to some other place; it was represented to his mind and spirit as if he had been taken up by the angel and carried through the air, just as Ezekiel was carried between earth and heaven, in the visions of God, to Jerusalem. On the array, take the purple and scarlet to express two things at once, her grandeur, authority and power, sitting as a queen and sovereign in the empire and ruling over kingdoms and nations, and also her bloody disposition towards the saints, with whose blood she is afterwards said to be drunk. On the name upon the forehead, set it first against its holy counterpart, since the high priest had upon his mitre, in that very place, the inscription holiness to the Lord, only of a wholly different import. Then give the custom the figure alludes to: harlots used not only to put their names over their doors but some of them upon their foreheads, so that all might know who they were, and proofs of this have been gathered out of four ancient authors. Draw the conclusion the figure is meant to yield, that this is expressive of openness and impudence in idolatrous worship, since she openly declares it, pleads for it, and invites and ensnares persons to join with her in it. On the drunkenness, let the shock of the image be felt rather than explained away. To see a woman drunk is a shameful sight; but to see one drunk, not with wine, but with blood, is monstrous and shocking; and not with her own blood, but the blood of others; and not the blood of wicked men, but of saints, whom God set apart from everlasting and whom Christ sanctified by his own blood.

Say what wilderness is meant, and be willing to be concrete: the country round about Rome is now a wilderness compared to what it once was. Then distinguish carefully between the woman and the beast she rides, for much depends on it. There is a very close connection between them, the seven heads of the beast being seven hills on which the woman sits; and yet there is a remarkable difference, the woman being the city with its buildings and inhabitants, especially the nobles, while the beast is the power that carries her. Note that the seer writes at first sight a beast, and not the beast, because the creature now appears different from before, bearing the bloody livery as well as the person of the woman; and that whereas he had before a name of blasphemy upon his head, he now has many. On the array, give the colours their civil meaning, purple and scarlet being the colours of the imperial habit, the purple in times of peace and the scarlet in times of war, and note that the golden cup answers to the cup of the ancient Babylon in Jeremiah, full of the most abominable doctrines as well as practices. On the inscription, observe that whereas the saints have the name of God and of the Lamb upon their foreheads, this name is of another kind; and that she is called the mother of harlots as the parent, ringleader, patroness and nourisher of many daughters who closely copy her, and the mother of abominations of every kind, spiritual and fleshly, and of the earth, that is, in all lands, in which respect she is indeed catholic or universal. On the last verse, say plainly that such a place may well be called the slaughter-house of the martyrs, and close where the seer closes, wondering exceedingly, at her cruelty and at the patience of God.

For the contrast: the woman is splendid and her surroundings desolate, and she is to be set against the woman clothed with the sun, driven into a wilderness and there persecuted but not forsaken
The text does not say; one interpreter takes the desert as symbolising the beast's future condition, another finds it in the state of the city at the rise of the papal power
It is the desolate state of the true Church in one wing of the once mighty empire

debates.question: What is the force of the name written on the forehead?

sides.position: Roman harlots wore a label bearing their names on their brows; and the redeemed by contrast bear God's name on theirs
The word mystery directs that Babylon be read mystically; but the printing in capitals answers to nothing in the original, and it is better rendered that a name was written, a mysterious name
The public inscription shows she is not ashamed but professes her doctrines openly, having refused to be ashamed

outliers.note: Alone sets the harlot against the woman clothed with the sun, observing that the persecuted woman was driven into a wilderness and there kept, while this one, amid all her dazzling surroundings, is still in a wilderness.

Alone insists on distinguishing the woman from the beast she rides, taking the woman for the city with its buildings and inhabitants and the beast for the power that carries her, and noting that the seer writes a beast and not the beast because the creature now wears the woman's bloody livery.

MYSTERY, BABYLON THE GREAT, THE MOTHER OF HARLOTS

7.pericope_label: The beast that was, and is not, and yet is

schools.summary: Take the angel's question as designed to relieve the seer rather than to reprove him: he stood fixed in astonishment, and the asking why he wondered was meant to show that the cause of the surprise was about to be removed, since the explanation now follows and runs to the end of the chapter. On the phrase was and is not, mark the tenses, an imperfect and a present, and note that the whole formula stands as an apparent antithesis to the description of God at the opening of the book as him who is and who was; it amounts, as has been said, to a parody of the divine name. Read the beast here as no longer simply the empire but as one of the emperors who died, who is going to come to life again, and observe that most interpreters find in this the current expectation of a returning Nero, thought to be realised in the emperor then reigning. Set out, however, exactly what the clause asserts, since it is easy to overstate it: there is a sense in which this power was, having existed before; a sense in which it is not, having become practically extinct; and a sense in which it still is, being so revived that it may be said to stand yet. On the ascent out of the abyss, take the meaning to be that the power would seem to come up from the nether world, appearing at one time extinct and then reviving as if from the realm over which Satan presides, and being in its revived character such as that origin would lead one to expect; and note that its end is destruction, that it will not be permanent but overthrown. On the wondering, mark the difference between the two amazements of this chapter, for the seer had wondered with the amazement of a horrible surprise, while the world will wonder and admire; and note that the thing will be so contrary to the regular course of events as to draw general attention.

Note that it is the same angel who has been speaking throughout, still carrying forward the interpretation he promised. Then take the phrase was, and is not, and yet is, and clear away the readings that will not stand before offering one that will. It is not to be understood of the devil, who was the god of this world and is cast out by Christ and yet is in being; for the dragon is expressly distinguished from this beast, and indeed it is from the dragon that the beast has his seat and power and authority. Nor is it to be understood of any particular emperor, such as the cruel and savage one who held power while another was abroad, was out of it upon that other's return, and afterwards was in again, as one sent from hell, going at last into perdition. Take it rather of the Roman empire itself, which carried and supported the Papacy; and note how variously even this may be applied, since the empire was in Roman hands originally and long continued so, and then in a sense was not, being in the hands of a Spaniard in the seer's own time, and yet was in being still, Rome remaining the metropolis of it. Let the reader see that the beast's identity survives all these changes of fortune, which is the very thing the threefold phrase is framed to say; and let him not be surprised that so much of the chapter has to be worked out by elimination, since the angel's explanation is itself given in terms that need explaining.

Say first what there was to astonish, for the seer's amazement is the hinge of the passage. The woman was drunk with the blood of the saints, while the beast which carried her abounded with sacred appellations, styles such as holy, most holy, most Christian, sacred and most sacred; and it is no wonder a man should stand amazed at that conjunction. The angel undertakes to explain the vision which had excited so great astonishment, and the explanation is of such importance that without it the mystery of the dragon and the beast could never have been satisfactorily explained in all its particulars. On the description itself, call it a very observable and punctual account, and set it out in its parts, since the whole duration of the beast is here divided into three periods and expressed in a fourfold manner: he was; and is not; and will ascend out of the bottomless pit and go into perdition. Note what the middle term means in practice, that when a vial had brought darkness upon his kingdom the woman took her advantage to seat herself upon him, and then it might well be said that he is not. Then note what the third term means, that he shall afterwards ascend with diabolical strength and fury, but will not reign long, going soon after his ascent into perdition for ever. And on the wondering of the earth, define the wonderers by what they lack: they are those whose names are not written in the book of life, men who prefer councils to divine revelation and take their religion from missals and rituals and legends instead of the sacred oracles, while those who abide by the Scriptures as the only rule of faith and practice are the exception.

Observe that here the mystery of the vision is explained, and observe also the limits of the explanation. The apostle wonders at the sight of this woman; the angel undertakes to open the vision to him, it being the key of the former visions; and he tells him what was meant by the beast on which the woman sat. Yet say honestly what follows, since a reader will find it out for himself if you do not: it is so explained as still to need further explanation. Then take the threefold phrase and give each member its sense. This beast was, that is, it was a seat of idolatry and persecution; and is not, that is, not in the ancient form, which was pagan; and yet it is, being truly the seat of idolatry and tyranny still, though of another sort and form. Note where it comes from and where it goes, for the two answer each other: it ascends out of the bottomless pit, since idolatry and cruelty are the issue and product of hell, and it shall return thither and go into perdition. Let the hearer take the point that the identity of a persecuting power is not in its outward shape, which may change entirely, but in what it does and what it loves; so that a man who is watching only for the old form will not recognise the thing when it returns in a new one. That is why the vision needed an angel to open it, and why, even when opened, it asks something of the reader still.

debates.question: What is the beast that was, and is not, and yet is?

sides.position: An emperor who died and is expected to live again; the phrase parodies the divine name, and most interpreters find here the expectation of a returning Nero
The Roman empire itself, which carried and supported the Papacy; neither the devil, who is distinguished from the beast, nor any single emperor
The Latin kingdom: it was, since Latinus was the first of those kings; it is not, since that nation ceased to be independent; and its ascent is therefore still future
A seat of idolatry and persecution, not in the ancient pagan shape, and yet truly that seat under another form
Three assertions only: that the power once was, that it had become practically extinct, and that it would so revive as to be said to stand yet
The inhabitants of the earth generally, the matter being so contrary to the regular course of events as to draw universal attention
Precisely those whose names are absent from the book of life, men who prefer councils to revelation and take their religion from missals and legends
The world, which will wonder and admire, in contrast with the seer, who wondered with the amazement of a horrible surprise

outliers.note: Alone admits the limits of the angel's own explanation, saying that the vision is opened to the apostle as the key of the former visions and yet is so explained as still to need further explanation.

Alone states what there was to astonish, that the woman was drunk with the blood of the saints while the beast which carried her abounded with sacred appellations, holy and most holy and most Christian and sacred.

themes: I will tell thee the mystery of the woman, and of the beast that carrieth her
The beast that thou sawest was, and is not; and shall ascend out of the bottomless pit
they that dwell on the earth shall wonder, whose names were not written in the book of life

9.pericope_label: The seven heads are seven mountains, and there are seven kings

schools.summary: Take the call for wisdom as a warning that what follows is not to be settled by ordinary minds or without earnest application; one rendering gives it, here is a meaning which comprises wisdom. Add that the wisdom asked for is partly of temper and not only of intellect, since it needs true wisdom to behold many incidents of the world's history and not find stumbling-blocks in them. On the seven mountains, take the plain reference, since Rome was known to its own poets as the city on seven hills, and note the shift in the imagery, that the heads which belonged to the beast are now the woman's, the beast carrying her. But do not let the literal basis close the meaning, for the explanation that follows widens it: the literalism is used to convey a broader symbolical sense, so that as Rome dwells on her seven hills, the world-city seen in vision sits among the various empires which have risen, like great mountains, in the history of the world. On the seven kings, set out the range of the word before choosing: it may denote a literal monarch, or any person of distinguished honour, or a dynasty or form of administration, and it would be contrary to the whole spirit of the passage to insist that it must mean literal kings and could not be applied to emperors or dictators or dynasties. Prefer that whole kingdoms are meant, and argue it from the vocabulary, since the verb used of the five that fell is the one employed for political catastrophe, of cities and of Babylon falling, whereas applied to individuals it would have to mean merely that they died; support it from Daniel, whose four beasts are called four kings and plainly represent kingdoms, and note that two great world-powers had preceded Daniel's four. Yet report the other view fairly, that the seven are men, admitting frankly that their identification is one of the puzzles of the book, that the counting is awkward because three emperors reigned too briefly to merit inclusion, and that the one who must continue a short space has been taken for the emperor who died after a reign of two years. On the eighth, be exact: when the seven heads fall no eighth head rises, but the beast, whose vitality has been seen in these successive heads, forms as it were an eighth which is out of the seven, not one of them but one rising from them; and note that the beast does not fall as the heads fall, but goes into destruction, a last power reserved for ruin.

Grant at the outset that this passage needs more than the angel's words to open it. Notwithstanding the interpretation given, a large share of wisdom is required, and there is enough here to exercise a mind ever so well stored with knowledge and understanding; one version renders the clause, here it is required that one should have judgment and wisdom, and another, this is the sense, he that hath wisdom, that is, let him make use of it and apply it to the proper persons, things and times. Then clear the ground of readings that cannot stand. The seven are not seven ages of the world, from Adam to Noah, from Noah to Abraham, from Abraham to David, from David to the captivity, from the captivity to Christ, from Christ to antichrist, and thence to the end, with the first five gone in the seer's time and the sixth then in being; that is a foolish and absurd interpretation, and it is made in the interest of taking the beast for the devil, whereas he is rather the head and god of this world. Nor are seven emperors of Rome intended, which different men reckon differently according to the date they assign the vision. On the eighth, say what it is and why it bears that name: it is the power which was in embryo in the seer's own day and had not yet come to its grandeur, and it takes the name of the beast because it is the head of the beast, and the only surviving head of a Roman empire now become Papal. Let the reader notice how much of this chapter has to be established by elimination, and let him hold the positive identification the more soberly for that.

Say plainly that only those who are wise will understand this, and that the call for wisdom is not a form of words. Then, on the seven mountains, refuse the merely antiquarian answer. Anciently there were royal palaces on all seven of the Roman hills; but the prophecy respects the seven hills as they stand at the time of the beast, when the older palace hill was deserted and another was in use. Note that the heads do not mean hills as distinct from kings, but have a compound meaning, implying both together. Then, if you will be particular, trace the succession of hills by the residences of the popes, observing that in the papal register the bulls of one period are dated from one palace and those of another period from another, and that no fifth or sixth or seventh hill has yet been the residence of any pope; and be candid that a hill was not deserted when another became the papal seat, but a new one added to the sacred palaces. On the number of the beast, hold that this passage cannot be satisfactorily explained until that number is first understood, since the same call for a mind that hath wisdom was made there. And on the mountains themselves, be willing to depart from the common reading: it has been objected that modern Rome does not stand upon those hills, and the word mountains may be taken figuratively, as it is elsewhere in this book and in the prophets, for great and mighty powers, so that the seven would be seven great eminences of dominion rather than seven pieces of ground. Let the hearer weigh which reading better fits the angel's own gloss that they are also seven kings.

sides.position: Rome, known to its own poets as the city on seven hills
Rome, but as a literal basis conveying a broader symbolical meaning, the world-city sitting among the empires that have risen like mountains in history
The hills as they stood under the papacy rather than in antiquity, the older palace hill deserted and another in use
Not Rome at all, since modern Rome does not stand so; mountains are to be taken figuratively, as elsewhere in the prophets, for seven great powers

debates.question: Are the seven kings men, or kingdoms?

sides.position: Kingdoms. The verb used of the five that fell is the one employed for political catastrophe, and applied to individuals it would have to mean merely that they died; Daniel's four beasts are called kings and plainly represent kingdoms
The word may denote a literal monarch, a person of distinguished honour, or a dynasty or form of administration, and it would be contrary to the spirit of the passage to insist on the narrowest sense
Men. The identification is one of the puzzles of the book, the counting awkward because three emperors reigned too briefly to include
Seven supreme forms of Latin government; since the heads are called kings as well, kingdoms cannot be what the mountains mean
Not an eighth head: when the seven fall the beast itself forms as it were an eighth, out of the seven but not one of them, and does not fall as the heads fall but goes into destruction
The emperor reigning as the seer wrote, reckoned among the seven because men thought him a second Nero, whose assassination was itself a symbol of the beast's end
The Papacy, the only surviving head of a Roman empire become Papal
The restoration of one of the seven, since to make a new head the form of government must differ in nature and in name
A power whose identity persists through every change, its last form so nearly prolonging the rest that it scarcely merited separate mention

outliers.note: Alone denies that the seven mountains refer to Rome at all, objecting that modern Rome does not stand upon those hills, and taking mountains figuratively, as the prophets use the word, for seven great powers.

Alone argues the case for kingdoms rather than men from the verb itself, since the word used of the five that fell is the one employed for political catastrophe, and applied to individual sovereigns it would be forced to mean merely that they died.

themes: The seven heads are seven mountains, on which the woman sitteth
there are seven kings: five are fallen, and one is, and the other is not yet come
the beast that was, and is not, even he is the eighth, and is of the seven

12.pericope_label: The ten horns are ten kings; these shall make war with the Lamb

schools.summary: Keep the heads and the horns distinct, since the chapter does. The heads are emperors and the horns are kings, both called by the same word, but the horns are compared to kings rather than identified with the emperors, succeeding them with something short of imperial power. Take them, consistently with the reading of the heads, not as personal sovereigns but as kingdoms or nationalities which had received no kingdom as yet, standing upon the seventh head, so that the hour of their power arrives only at the fall of the sixth. Note that they were not in existence when this was written, and that the one hour cannot be literal but marks something brief and provisional, a form of administration afterwards succeeded by more settled ones, which answers exactly to the governments thrown up after the incursion of the northern barbarians, most of which were short-lived and were soon remodelled into permanent states. On their being of one mind, take it as one purpose, and mark the symmetry of the arrangement: as the dragon gave his power and authority to the beast, so these are now wholly at the beast's service. Draw the observation that carries beyond the first century, that though they are sundered powers they are one in their subjection, and that the idea of a universal empire may disappear while the spirit and principle of mere earthliness remains, so that no power the size of Rome is needed to illustrate that spirit. On the war with the Lamb, note that the title given here, Lord of lords and King of kings, is given to Christ again later in this book and to God in the Law and in Daniel, so that crowned heads are Christ's subjects. Then answer the question when this war is made, and answer it morally rather than by a date: they make war whenever the direction of their policy and their morals is in favour of oppression, wrong and worldliness, for whenever nations allow the secular spirit to breathe through all they do, they are not with Christ but against him, though there are hints besides that some special outbreak of hostility may take place. Note last that those with him shall also overcome, sharing the triumph as they shared the conflict, and that called and chosen and faithful are the three notes of such as share it.

Settle first who the ten kings are not, since the field is full of guesses. They are not ten Christian emperors reckoned from Constantine to Theodosius, for these did not reign with the beast, nor give their kingdoms to him, and much less did they make war with the Lamb; they are rather to be numbered with the angels that fought for the Lamb against the dragon. Neither are they ten kings that shall rise up and divide the Roman empire between them towards the end of the world, a sense devised to obscure and hide from men the true meaning of the passage. Take them rather for the ten kingdoms which rose up when the Roman empire was ruined and torn to pieces by the Goths, the Huns and the Vandals, and identify them with the ten toes of the image in Nebuchadnezzar's dream and the ten horns of the fourth beast in Daniel. Be candid that interpreters reckon them differently, one naming Spain, France, Lombardy, England, Scotland, Denmark, Sweden, Hungary, Italy and the exarchate of Ravenna, while another lists them otherwise. On their being of one mind, take the unity to be religious and gradual: the princes of these kingdoms and their subjects became in time of one religion, first Arians and then Papists, and for a long series of time there was great unity between them in their attachment to that church, its principles and its practices. On the war with the Lamb, deny that a personal war or a final battle is meant, and refer it instead to a war with his members, that is, the persecuting of the saints and of the faithful witnesses of Christ in all ages, within the jurisdictions of these kings and at the instigation of the beast under whose influence they are.

Take the ten horns as ten kingdoms yet in futurity when this was written, and note the force of the clause that they had received no dominion as yet, since the part of the empire then in power was the sixth head, the imperial government of the heathen Caesars. Render the phrase about one hour rather as one time, so that these states receive dominion at the same time as the beast, and their reign is concurrent with his rather than merely brief. On their giving their power and strength to him, draw the inference that the ten horns must constitute the principal strength of that empire, which is therefore composed of the dominions of ten monarchs independent of each other in every sense except their implicit obedience to the church that rides upon it; and note that the beast is here distinguished from its horns, as the whole is distinguished in history from its constituent powers. On the war with the Lamb, say what it consists in, since no one imagines these kings drew up in battle against Christ in person: they make war upon him by persecuting his followers, and this has been true of every state so constituted, which has constantly opposed the progress of pure Christianity so long as it had secular power. Then state the two things that follow, and keep them in this order. First, that these kings are nevertheless God's ministers to execute his vengeance upon the idolatrous nations, since no lord has authority but from Christ and no king reigns without him. Second, that when these monarchies have executed the divine purpose, those that are with the Lamb, the called and the chosen and the faithful, those who have kept the truth in the love of it, shall prevail against all their adversaries, because their battles are fought by the Lamb, who is their God and their deliverer.

Set the war before the hearer as a contest in which appearances and outcome are opposite, for that is the whole force of the verse. Here is a war begun between the beast and his followers on the one side and the Lamb and his followers on the other; and the beast and his army, to an eye of sense, appear much stronger than the Lamb and his army, so that one would think an army with a Lamb at the head of them could not stand before the great red dragon. Then declare the victory: the Lamb shall overcome, for Christ must reign till all enemies be put under his feet, and though he will be sure to meet with many enemies and much opposition, he will also be sure to gain the victory. Then give the ground of the victory, and give it twice. It is taken first from the character of the Lamb, who is King of kings and Lord of lords, having both by nature and by office supreme dominion and power over all things, so that all the powers of earth and hell are subject to his check and control. It is taken second from the character of his followers, who are called and chosen and faithful: called out by commission to this warfare, chosen and fitted for it, and faithful in it. Close by putting the two together, for the encouragement lies in the combination and not in either half alone: such an army, under such a commander, will at length carry all the world before them.

sides.position: Kingdoms or nationalities, not personal sovereigns, whose hour arrives at the fall of the sixth head
Kings compared to kings rather than identified with the emperors, succeeding them with something short of imperial power

The kingdoms into which the empire broke when the Goths and Vandals tore it, the same as the ten toes of the image and the ten horns of Daniel's fourth beast; not Christian emperors from Constantine to Theodosius, nor kings postponed to the end of the world
Ten Latin kingdoms still future when this was written, receiving dominion at the same time as the beast
Kingdoms not yet in existence, the hour marking something brief and provisional, as with the governments thrown up after the northern invasions

debates.question: When do these powers make war with the Lamb?

sides.position: Whenever the direction of their policy and morals favours oppression, wrong and worldliness; nations that let the secular spirit breathe through all they do are against him
Not in a personal or final battle, but in the persecution of Christ's members in every age
Not by open proclamation of war, but by sustaining a persecuting power

outliers.note: Alone answers the question when the war against the Lamb is made in moral rather than chronological terms, holding that it is made whenever the policy of nations favours oppression and worldliness, and adding that the idea of a universal empire may disappear while the spirit of mere earthliness remains.

Alone clears the ground by elimination before identifying the ten, rejecting both the reckoning that makes them Christian emperors from Constantine to Theodosius and the reading that postpones them to the end of the world.

themes: the ten horns which thou sawest are ten kings, which have received no kingdom as yet
These have one mind, and shall give their power and strength unto the beast
These shall make war with the Lamb, and the Lamb shall overcome them

15.pericope_label: The waters are peoples; the ten horns shall hate the whore

schools.summary: Take the explanation of the waters as a key to the imagery used elsewhere in the book, and note that the Old Testament had long employed waters as a symbol for peoples. Observe that outspread seas or raging floods would naturally represent such multitudes, and that the four terms mark diversity as well as number, so that perhaps under no single earlier government, neither Babylonian nor Macedonian nor ancient Roman, was there so great a variety of peoples speaking so many different tongues. Then draw the point that both the wild beast and the harlot draw much of their power from the people, since the easily-moved passions of a fickle crowd, and its generous unreasoning impulses, are exactly what subtle and seductive enemies use; and remember the saying that men never so much need to be theocratic as when they are most democratic, for a newly discovered strength is what unscrupulous ambition will make its tool. On the turning of the horns, note the surprise, since these same powers were lately in alliance with the beast and gave it all their strength, so that what is said here must belong to a later period and mark a great change of feeling and policy. Keep the picture exact: she was seen in splendid apparel riding the beast, and now the beast turns with the ten horns of his power upon her, makes her deserted, strips her of her adornments, consumes the spoil, which is what eating her flesh means, and burns her with fire. Note that the downfall will come from a sudden change in the subject peoples, and that the seer wrote before the days of Alaric and Genseric and the hordes that devastated Rome, so that no reader of the later historians will be at a loss for materials to illustrate the prophecy. On the last verse, say that the woman is the great city which has a kingdom over the kings of the earth, and that with these words the angel's explanation of the mystery ends; but leave the door open, for Rome followed Babylon, and other cities may follow in their train.

Note that the angel is still carrying forward the interpretation he undertook, and take the ten horns here to include both the particular kings and states which have defended that power and the whole empire which has borne it up. Then, on the clause that God put it in their hearts, distinguish the senses of the divine will at work, since the whole weight of the passage rests there. It is his approving will, what he likes of and will be well pleased with; it is his will of command, what he will order to be done; and it is his determining will, his will of purpose and decree, what he has resolved shall be done. Say what follows from that last sense, that he has fixed the time of her reign, and that longer than that she shall not continue. Then state the relation between the divine purpose and the human agents plainly, and do not soften either side of it. These kings, in destroying her, will not do so much their own will as the will of God; God will put it into their hearts to do it, working in them both to will and to do, filling them with hatred to her, inclining their minds to the thing as it will be in the power of their hands to do it. He who has the hearts of all men, and even of kings, in his hands, and can turn them as rivers of water, will move them to it, as he turned the hearts of the Egyptians before. Let the reader see that their hatred is real hatred and their act their own, and that it is nevertheless the accomplishing of a decree older than their kingdoms.

Take the plurals in the angel's explanation as marking the extent of her jurisdiction, so many words in the plural number fitly denoting the great extensiveness of her power; and note that she herself glories in the title of the Catholic Church and exults in the number of her votaries as a certain proof of the true religion, one controversialist having made the very name his first note of the true Church and amplitude, or multitude and variety of believers, his fourth. Then find in the sixteenth verse a clue to the right interpretation of the horns. Since the ten are to hate the harlot, and this must be connected with what follows, the meaning is that the ten kingdoms in her interest shall finally despise her doctrines, be reformed from her, assist in depriving her of all influence, and in the end consign her to destruction. From that it follows, and the inference is worth pressing, that no power which did not still exist at the Reformation can be numbered among the horns; the ten must therefore be found among the great states of Europe at its commencement, and they were exactly ten. On the seventeenth verse, let no one imagine that these kingdoms, because they support an idolatrous worship, have been raised up merely by the power of man or the chances of war. No kingdom or state can exist without the will of God; therefore let the inhabitants of the world tremble when they see a wicked monarchy rise to power, and let them consider that it is raised up by the Lord to execute his vengeance upon the idolatries and profligacies of the times. And on the last verse, note that the woman is called a city, which is a much plainer emblem of a Church, the word being used unequivocally in that sense in many parts of Scripture.

State the doctrine of providence which this passage teaches, and state it without qualification, for the passage does. God so ruled the hearts of these kings, by his power over them and by his providence, that they did those things, without intending it, which he purposed and foretold. Then say what the kings themselves will come to see, since the text implies a reckoning: they shall see their folly, and how they have been bewitched and enslaved by the harlot, and shall be made instruments in her destruction. Observe what becomes of a fellowship founded on sin, and let it stand as a warning about all such fellowships: their joining together in sin will be turned to hatred and rage, and they will eagerly assist in tormenting each other. On the identification, be brief and firm, since the vision itself is explicit: she was that great city which reigned over the kings of the earth when the apostle had this vision, and every one knows which city that was. Then close the chapter where its comfort lies, and let the two destinies be set side by side. Believers will be received to the glory of the Lord, when wicked men will be destroyed in a most awful manner. But the Lord's portion is his people; his counsel shall stand, and he will do all his pleasure, to his own glory and to the happiness of all his servants.

debates.question: What follows from the waters being peoples?

sides.position: That both beast and harlot draw their power from the people, the passions of a fickle crowd being what subtle enemies use; men never so much need to be theocratic as when they are most democratic
That vast numbers of differing nations and tongues were subject to this power, a diversity greater than any earlier government had gathered
That the plurals mark the extent of a jurisdiction which glories in the title Catholic and counts the number of her adherents a proof of the true religion
That Rome's greatest danger lay in the very multitudes under her sway

debates.question: How is the horns' turning against the harlot to be explained?

sides.position: There is an apparent incongruity with their earlier alliance, so this must belong to a later period and mark a great change of policy
It supplies the clue to the horns themselves: since they are to be reformed from her, no power that had ceased before the Reformation can be one of them
The beast turns his own horns upon her, strips and consumes and burns her, other kingdoms rising who hate her tyranny and covet her wealth
The downfall came from a sudden change in the subject peoples, the seer writing before Alaric and Genseric

outliers.note: Alone draws from the waters a warning about popular power itself, that the easily-moved passions of a crowd are what subtle and seductive enemies use, and quotes the saying that men never so much need to be theocratic as when they are most democratic.
Alone leaves the identification open at the end, observing that Rome followed Babylon and that other cities may follow in their train.
